title: NASA Moves SunRISE Solar Mission From Grounded Vulcan Rocket to SpaceX Falcon Heavy
excerpt: The payload switch is the latest blow to ULA as its Vulcan rocket remains sidelined by a solid rocket booster anomaly, with the Space Force already having reassigned multiple national security launches to SpaceX.
body:
• NASA announced it is moving the SunRISE heliophysics mission from ULA's Vulcan Centaur rocket to SpaceX's Falcon Heavy, citing ULA's ongoing grounding.
  • The SunRISE mission, which will deploy six cubesats to study the Sun's corona, was originally scheduled for launch in summer 2026 but will now ride as a Space Force rideshare payload, with the next Falcon Heavy flight set for 2027.
  • ULA's Vulcan has been grounded since a solid rocket booster nozzle anomaly during the USSF-87 launch on February 12, and repairs appear stalled.
  • The Space Force has already reassigned multiple GPS and national security satellite launches from Vulcan to SpaceX, costing ULA significant revenue.

NASA has switched the launch vehicle for its SunRISE solar science mission from United Launch Alliance's grounded Vulcan Centaur rocket to SpaceX's Falcon Heavy, the agency announced this week. The move is the latest in a growing list of payloads stripped from ULA as the company struggles to return its flagship rocket to flight after a booster anomaly grounded it five months ago.

The SunRISE (Sun Radio Interferometer Space Experiment) mission will deploy six cubesats to form a space-based radio interferometer, mapping how the Sun generates and releases giant particle storms that can threaten satellites, astronauts and power grids on Earth. It will now fly as a rideshare payload sponsored by the U.S. Space Force's Space Systems Command, with the next Falcon Heavy launch scheduled for 2027.

Why Vulcan Is Grounded

ULA's Vulcan rocket has not flown since the USSF-87 mission on February 12, when one of its four GEM 63XL solid rocket boosters, built by Northrop Grumman, suffered a nozzle anomaly about 65 seconds after liftoff. The rocket's core stage compensated and successfully delivered its Space Force payload to geosynchronous orbit, but the incident — the second nozzle failure across Vulcan's short flight history — prompted the Pentagon to ground the vehicle for national security missions pending investigation.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DafQiQkHL8z/

"ULA hopes to resume flights using boosters with the new design before year's end, and is separately preparing a boosterless Vulcan configuration for Amazon satellite launches."

Northrop Grumman completed a successful static-fire test of a redesigned nozzle on April 15, but the investigation remains ongoing. ULA hopes to resume flights using boosters with the new design before year's end, and is separately preparing a boosterless Vulcan configuration for Amazon satellite launches. The company took a $71 million charge related to the anomaly in its most recent quarterly earnings.

A Cascade of Lost Missions

The SunRISE switch adds to a growing list of payloads redirected from Vulcan. The Space Force has already moved at least three GPS satellite launches to SpaceX, and is assessing further shifts for next-generation missile warning satellites, wideband communications spacecraft and National Reconnaissance Office intelligence payloads that had been manifested on Vulcan.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=G1gGo8yDjTI

"I'm going to look for every flexibility I have to make sure that I can deliver warfighter capability as quickly as possible. Until this anomaly is solved, we will not be launching national security space launch missions on Vulcan."

— Lt. Gen. Douglas Schiess, Deputy Chief of Space Operations

The situation comes just days after the Space Force awarded $17 billion in new NSSL Phase 3 Lane 1 contracts to seven companies — including SpaceX, ULA, Blue Origin, Rocket Lab and three newer entrants — but SpaceX remains the only provider with an operational NSSL-certified rocket. Blue Origin's New Glenn was damaged in a static-fire test explosion in May.

Implications for the Launch Market

The ongoing Vulcan grounding has effectively turned the U.S. national security launch market into a SpaceX near-monopoly. While ULA continues to launch Amazon satellites using its retiring Atlas-5 rocket — with only about seven vehicles remaining in inventory — the company's commercial prospects depend on resolving the Vulcan booster issue.

For NASA, the switch to Falcon Heavy as a rideshare means it loses direct control over launch timing, but gains a proven vehicle that has completed multiple national security and science missions. The trade-off mirrors a broader shift across the U.S. space enterprise: when schedules matter more than procurement tradition, the payload goes to SpaceX.
